title: An Assessment of Psychological Noise Reduction by Landscape Plants
research_question: To study the psychological benefits provided by urban parks and other landscape environments, combining subjective (questionnaire) and objective (EEG) approaches to assess psychological noise reduction by landscape plants and its effects on health benefits and psychological behavior.

participants.description: 20 female and 20 male students from Zhejiang Forestry University, aged 21 to 25 years (average age 23 years).
participants.recruitment: Participants were randomly selected within the university and given a simple oral introduction to the survey methods before being invited to participate.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three-minute video clip of a busy road traffic scene (Site A, Nanshan Road, Hangzhou) showing road traffic and passers-by.
Three-minute video clip of a vegetation scene (Site B, next to Nanshan Road, Hangzhou) showing hedges, lawns, and other vegetation forms in street parks with people walking.
Recorded traffic noise, standardized to an LAeq value of 68.6 dB, played during both video conditions (Site A and Site B).
Baseline (BC) condition: Participants wore video glasses and EEG equipment, but no video or noise was presented.

measures.construct: Belief in landscape plants' contribution to noise reduction
Perceived effectiveness of different noise barriers
Perceived noise attenuation by landscape plants

measures.instrument: Electroencephalogram (EEG) measuring power in delta (0.1–3.5 Hz), theta (4–7.5 Hz), alpha-1 (8–11.0 Hz), alpha-2 (11.5-13.5 Hz), beta-1 (14–18.5 Hz), and beta-2 (19–30 Hz) frequency bands at 16 electrode locations (C3, C4, F3, F4, F7, F8, Fp1, Fp2, O1, O2, P3, P4, T3, T4, T5, T6).

measures.construct: Subjective emotional evaluation (response to unpleasant noise)
Evaluation of living environment acoustical condition

findings.consequent: Belief that landscape plants contribute to noise reduction
findings.mechanism: Visual stimuli partially influence the psychological apperception of acoustic perceptions.
findings.quote: 90% of the subjects believed that landscape plants could contribute to noise reduction

findings.antecedent: Type of noise barrier (plant hedges vs. concrete/plastic/metal)
findings.mechanism: Visual stimuli partially influence the psychological apperception of acoustic perceptions.
findings.quote: 80% of the participants indicated that plant hedges were the most effective noise barriers.

findings.antecedent: Visual presence of landscape plants (hedge between traffic and park)
findings.consequent: Overrated perceived noise attenuation (psychological noise reduction)
findings.mechanism: The overrated noise attenuation caused by a person's subjectivity can be described as a psychological noise reduction.
findings.quote: They overrated the plants' ability to attenuate noise... described as a psychological noise reduction.

findings.antecedent: Visual scene (Traffic vs. Vegetation) + Noise (68.6 dB)
findings.consequent: Beta-1 EEG power at F3, F4, F7, F8, Fp1, Fp2, O1, O2, P3, P4, T3, T4
findings.mechanism: Associated with elevated negative emotions, withdrawal and/or anxiety.
findings.quote: Both beta-1 and beta-2 power at F3, F4, F7, F8, Fp1, Fp2, O1 and O2 increased significantly more in the traffic scene group than in the vegetation scene group or BC group (P < 0.05).

findings.antecedent: Visual scene (Traffic vs. Vegetation) + Noise (68.6 dB)
findings.consequent: Beta-2 EEG power at F3, F4, F7, F8, Fp1, Fp2, O1, O2, P3, P4, T3, T4, T5, T6
findings.mechanism: Associated with elevated negative emotions, withdrawal and/or anxiety.
findings.quote: Both beta-1 and beta-2 power at F3, F4, F7, F8, Fp1, Fp2, O1 and O2 increased significantly more in the traffic scene group than in the vegetation scene group or BC group (P < 0.05).

findings.antecedent: Visual scene (Traffic or Vegetation) + Noise (68.6 dB) vs. Baseline (BC)
findings.quote: At this site, both the traffic scene group and the vegetation scene group decreased significantly more than did the BC group (P < 0.05).

findings.antecedent: Visual scene (Traffic) + Noise (68.6 dB) vs. Baseline (BC)
findings.consequent: Theta EEG power (at electrodes other than C3, C4)
findings.mechanism: Strong theta band increases during concentrated task performance and memory operations.
findings.quote: However, there was a significant difference in values between the traffic scene and BC groups except for the central sites (C3, C4).

findings.antecedent: Visual scene (Traffic vs. Vegetation) + Noise (68.6 dB)
findings.quote: There were no significant differences in the theta band between the traffic scene and the vegetation scene groups at any electrodes

findings.antecedent: Visual scene (Vegetation) + Noise (68.6 dB) vs. Baseline (BC)
findings.quote: and the vegetation scene and BC groups also failed to reach significance.

findings.antecedent: Visual scene (Vegetation vs. Traffic) + Noise (68.6 dB)
findings.consequent: Alpha EEG activity (alpha-1 and alpha-2 relative percentum)
findings.mechanism: Higher alpha percentage indicates a positively perceived emotional difference, consistent with stress recovery and restoration.
findings.quote: There was significantly less alpha activity in the vegetation scene than in the traffic scene at frontopolar, central, parietal and occipital regions.

findings.antecedent: Visual scene (Traffic vs. Vegetation) + Noise (68.6 dB)
findings.consequent: Beta EEG activity (beta-1 and beta-2 relative percentum)
findings.mechanism: Lower beta percentage indicates a positively perceived emotional difference, consistent with reduced negative emotions, withdrawal, and/or anxiety.
findings.quote: Furthermore, beta activity increased significantly more with the traffic scene than with the plant scene at all sites except T3, T4.

findings.consequent: Right hemisphere EEG activity (all frequency bands)
findings.mechanism: Greater right hemisphere activity may be associated with elevated negative emotions, withdrawal and/or anxiety.
findings.quote: the right hemisphere was more emotionally active than the left for all frequency bands because both the EEG power (Table 1) and the percent fluctuation (Table 2) of the even electrodes located on the right hemisphere were larger than those of the odd electrodes located on the left hemisphere.

mechanisms: Psychological noise reduction: visual stimuli (landscape plants) influence the psychological apperception of acoustic perceptions, leading to an overestimation of noise attenuation.
Emotional processing: changes in EEG frequency bands (synchronization of beta, desynchronization of alpha) reflect emotional responses to visual and auditory stimuli.
Restorative effects: green spaces lead to higher alpha and lower beta activity, indicating a positively perceived emotional difference and stress recovery.
Lateralization of emotion: greater right hemisphere EEG activity is associated with elevated negative emotions, withdrawal, and/or anxiety.
implementation_implications: Landscape plants provide excess noise attenuation through subjects' emotional processing, supporting their use in green transportation systems.
Green environments in slow transport systems (roadside green space) can moderate tension from traffic noise and increase walking trips.
Assessing intangible services and benefits of green infrastructure is crucial for urban sustainability strategies.

tables.description: Mean values of EEG power (µV²) for delta, theta, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 frequency bands across 16 electrodes (C3, C4, F3, F4, F7, F8, Fp1, Fp2, O1, O2, P3, P4, T3, T4, T5, T6) for three conditions (BC, Traffic scene, Plant scene).
key_stats: differences are significant at P < 0.05 according to a Tukey's test.

tables.description: Results of an ANOVA for the relative per centum of the six frequency EEG bands (delta, theta, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, beta-2) across 16 electrodes for Traffic scene and Plant scene conditions, relative to the BC set.

limitations: The study sample consisted only of students from Zhejiang Forestry University, which is a biased sample.

The study did not include citizens most affected by urban noise (e.g., children, elderly, those living near main roads), potentially neglecting individual differences in physiological function due to age.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The emphasis in the term ‘Green Transportation’ is on the word ‘green’. Green transportation focuses on the construction of a slow transport system with a visually pleasing, easy and secure trip environment composed of urban parks, green roadside spaces and some other space that is full of landscape plants. This trip environment encourages residents to make trip choices that reduce fuel consumption and pollution and is one of the most important ways of popularizing green transportation. To study the psychological benefits provided by urban parks and other landscape environments, we combined a subjective approach (a questionnaire) with an objective quantitative approach (emotional tests using an electroencephalogram; EEG). Using a questionnaire survey, we found that 90% of the subjects believed that landscape plants contribute to noise reduction and that 55% overrated the plants’ actual ability to attenuate noise. Two videos (showing a traffic scene and a plant scene) were shown to 40 participants on video glasses. We detected and recorded EEG values with a portable electroencephalograph, and a comparison between the results of the two groups revealed that there was a highly significant asymmetry between the EEG activity of the vegetation scene and traffic scene groups. The results suggest that the emotions aroused by noise and visual stimuli are manifested in the synchronization of beta frequency band and the desynchronization of alpha frequency band, indicating that landscape plants can moderate or buffer the effects of noise. These findings indicate that landscape plants provide excess noise attenuating effects through subjects’ emotional processing, which we term ‘psychological noise reduction’.
